concept.name: Clearing fee
concept.definition: The fee charged by a clearing organization (central counterparty) for clearing and settling a trade - standing between buyer and seller, managing margin and default risk, and effecting final settlement. It is charged per contract or per trade to clearing members and passed through to customers.
concept.intuition: After the trade, someone has to guarantee both sides perform; the clearing fee pays the clearinghouse for being that guarantor.
concept.mechanics: Clearing agencies publish fee schedules filed with regulators; e.g., OCC charges a per-contract clearing fee ($0.025 as of January 2025, previously with a flat $55 cap for very large transactions), set under its capital management policy to cover operating expenses and risk buffers. Futures clearing works similarly at CME and other DCOs on a per-contract basis.
concept.formula: Clearing fee = per-contract rate x number of contracts (e.g., $0.025/contract at OCC).
concept.failure_modes: Clearing fees are small but unavoidable on every cleared trade and scale linearly with contract volume, mattering most to high-turnover derivatives strategies. They also change by regulatory filing on notice, so cost models must track fee schedules.
concept.misconceptions: Clearing fees are not exchange fees or broker commissions - they compensate the CCP's guarantee and settlement function, a different entity with its own schedule. They apply even on 'commission-free' trades in cleared products.
concept.example: A 100-lot listed options trade incurs a $2.50 OCC clearing fee at $0.025 per contract, on top of any exchange execution fee and broker commission.

citations.source: Federal Register: OCC Notice of Filing - Schedule of Fees update (SR-OCC-2024-017)
citations.section: Per Contract Clearing Fee ($0.02 to $0.025) and fee structure
